title: App Distribution, Releases & Compatibility
summary: You can't force-update every install, and the app store sits between you and your users. Learn why that forces staged rollouts, remote config, and years of API back-compat.

slides.markdown:
Deploy a backend fix and every request hits the new code within minutes. Ship a mobile fix and, months later, a meaningful slice of your users are still running the version before it — some by choice, some because their region's app store review is slow, some because they simply never open the update prompt.

That single constraint — **you cannot force everyone onto your latest client** — reshapes release process, API design, and how bugs get fixed. This topic covers why mobile releases aren't like deploying a server, the store review gate, staged rollouts and kill switches, and designing APIs that tolerate years of old clients still calling them. CI/CD pipeline mechanics themselves live in Engineering Craft and Cloud & DevOps.

slides.sectionTitle: Why mobile releases aren't like deploying a web server
slides.markdown:
A backend deploy replaces the running code atomically — old requests briefly straddle the transition, but within minutes every request is served by the new version. There is one "current" version, and you control when it goes live and can roll it back in seconds.

A mobile release has none of that. Once a version is on a device, it stays there until the user chooses to update — no push mechanism exists to force it. That means at any given moment your backend is serving a **mix of every client version you've shipped in the past several years**, not a clean before/after. A change that assumes "everyone's on the new version now" a week after release is a change built on a false premise; a meaningful fraction of your traffic is often still on versions from a year or more ago.

Every other point in this topic — review gates, staged rollouts, backward-compatible APIs — is a direct consequence of that one structural fact.

slides.sectionTitle: The app store review pipeline and what it means for release timing
slides.markdown:
Unlike a backend deploy, a mobile release passes through a **third party's review gate** before it reaches any user — Apple's App Store review and Google Play's review, each with their own timeline (hours to a few days typically, longer for a first submission or a policy-sensitive change) and their own rejection criteria you don't fully control.

The direct consequence: your release timeline has an external, variable-length dependency you can't schedule around precisely. Teams build slack into their release calendar for this — submitting a day or more ahead of a planned release date, and never planning a hotfix that assumes same-day approval, because review time is genuinely unpredictable and can reject for reasons unrelated to the actual bug you're fixing.

This is also why remote config and feature flags (below) matter so much more on mobile than on a backend: they let you change behavior **without** going through review again, for anything that doesn't require new native code.

slides.sectionTitle: Staged rollouts and kill switches for a bad release
slides.markdown:
Both stores let you release to a **percentage** of eligible users rather than everyone at once — 1%, then 10%, then 50%, then 100%, watching crash rate and key metrics at each stage before widening. A regression caught at 1% affects a small fraction of users and can be halted by pausing the rollout; the same regression released at 100% affects everyone before anyone notices.

A staged rollout only helps if you're actually watching a real-time signal during it — crash-free rate, a key funnel metric — and have a clear threshold for pausing, not just a plan to "check back tomorrow." A rollout that's fire-and-forget provides none of the protection the staging was meant to buy.

A **kill switch** (a remote flag your app checks that can disable a specific feature entirely) complements this for the case a bug ships anyway: if the broken feature is gated behind a remote flag, you can turn it off for everyone instantly, without waiting for a new release to clear review — the only fast mitigation path mobile actually has once something's live.

slides.sectionTitle: A rollout with a canary percentage and rollback
slides.markdown:
A healthy staged rollout has a decision point at every stage, not just a schedule: release to 1% → hold and watch crash-free rate and key metrics for a defined window → if healthy, widen to 10% → repeat → 50% → 100%. At any stage, a metric crossing a pre-agreed threshold triggers an immediate pause or full halt, not "widen anyway since we're already committed."

Rollback on mobile doesn't mean reverting code the way a backend does — the previous version is still what most users are running, since the rollout only ever reached a fraction of the base. "Rollback" here means **halting the rollout** so the bad version's exposure stops growing, then, if the bug is severe enough for users already on the new version, flipping a kill switch for the specific broken feature while a real fix goes through review.

slides.sectionTitle: Feature flags and remote config on mobile
slides.markdown:
Remote config is a small, server-hosted key-value store your app fetches and checks, letting you change app behavior — enable a feature, adjust a limit, turn something off — **without a new app release or another trip through store review**. This is the primary tool mobile teams have for reacting fast to something a normal backend team would just redeploy for.

The pattern that makes this safe: any risky new feature ships **behind a flag, defaulted off**, in the same build as everything else — the code is in the release, but inert until the flag flips. This decouples "the code is out in the world" from "the feature is active," which matters enormously given how slowly old client code disappears — a flag can be flipped back off in seconds if something's wrong, while the alternative (a broken feature baked in with no flag) requires a full release cycle, including review, to fix.

The trade-off: every flag is a permanent code branch until it's cleaned up, and flag debt that never gets removed is a real, recurring source of mobile codebase complexity — treat "remove the flag once it's fully rolled out" as part of the feature's definition of done, not a someday task.

slides.sectionTitle: Designing APIs that tolerate years of old clients
slides.markdown:
Because a version from three years ago might still be calling your API today, backend changes serving mobile clients need a **backward-compatibility discipline** that a backend-only team calling its own internal services doesn't have to think about nearly as hard.

The concrete rules: never remove a field an old client reads — deprecate and stop *writing new data into it* if needed, but don't delete it out from under a client that still parses it; never make a previously-optional field required, since old clients won't send it; version breaking changes explicitly (a new endpoint or an API version header) rather than mutating an existing contract in place; and always include a client version identifier in requests so you can measure exactly how much traffic is still on old versions before making any change that touches back-compat, rather than guessing.

The discipline pays off precisely because you can't fix a broken old client — it's not getting a hotfix. The only lever you have is not breaking it in the first place, or, if a version genuinely must be cut off, doing so deliberately with a minimum-supported-version check server-side rather than an accidental API change quietly breaking it.

slides.sectionTitle: Shipping a breaking API change assuming everyone updates fast
slides.markdown:
A backend team ships a change that renames a response field or changes its type, reasoning that "the app team already released the update that handles this a week ago, so it should be fine by now." A week later, the old field format is still being requested by every client that hasn't updated — often a substantial fraction of the active base — and those clients start crashing or silently misbehaving on the changed response.

This mistake usually comes from a team used to backend-to-backend deploys, where "we released the fix" and "everyone's using it" are nearly the same statement within minutes. On mobile they are never the same statement — release and adoption are decoupled by weeks or months, and adoption never reaches 100% for any given version at all, since some fraction of users are permanently on old hardware that can't take the latest OS or app version.

The fix isn't "wait longer" — it's not making the breaking change unversioned at all. Add a new field or endpoint version alongside the old one, keep the old contract alive for as long as any supported client version might call it, and use real client-version telemetry, not a release-date guess, to decide when it's actually safe to retire the old path.

slides.sectionTitle: Relying on a forced-update prompt as the only compatibility strategy
slides.markdown:
Some teams handle the "old clients still exist" problem by shipping a forced-update screen — a blocking dialog that prevents using the app below some minimum version — and treating that as their entire back-compat strategy: "we'll just make everyone update."

The gap: a forced update only helps users who **can** update. Someone on an old OS version their device can't upgrade past, someone in a region with slow or expensive data, someone who simply hasn't opened the app in weeks and hits the block cold with no warning — all of them are now fully locked out, often mid-task, with no path forward except a device they may not be willing or able to replace. This converts a compatibility problem into a support and churn problem, and it disproportionately affects users on older, cheaper devices — often a business's most price-sensitive and least able to simply buy a new phone.

Forced updates are a legitimate last resort for a genuine security issue, not a substitute for designing APIs and features that degrade gracefully on older clients in the first place. Use it sparingly, and pair it with the softest version — a dismissible "please update soon" nudge — for everything short of an actual emergency.
